overview: The City Council Planning and Permitting Committee is a standing committee of the Medford City Council responsible for evaluating and drafting municipal zoning updates, land-use policies, and property-related ordinances. Its work centers on modernizing the city's zoning code to encourage walkable mixed-use growth, increase housing capacity, establish environmental performance standards, and regulate vacant and converted properties. Across twenty-six meetings from August 2024 through May 2026, the committee reviewed comprehensive district-by-district rezoning proposals developed alongside municipal staff and planning consultants. At its most recent meeting in May 2026, the committee referred an amended zoning proposal for the Boston Avenue corridor to the full City Council for a joint hearing with the Community Development Board while continuing discussions on institutional zoning for Tufts University.

threads.name: Mystic Avenue Corridor Rezoning
threads.summary: In August 2024, consultants Innes Associates presented a zoning overhaul framework for Mystic Avenue recommending curb setbacks, widened sidewalks, and building heights up to twelve stories in exchange for active ground floors (M01#1). Planning staff requested early draft text and design standards to evaluate the technical feasibility of the proposed curb setbacks (M01#2). In September 2024, the committee approved directives instructing consultants to draft language utilizing Option B with incentive zoning, add life sciences, and adjust parcel configurations (M03#3). The committee reviewed dimensional standards and map adjustments for auto-oriented parcels in October 2024 (M04#2). Later that month, the committee finalized the draft proposal establishing four sub-districts and development incentives, voting to refer the Mystic Avenue Corridor District zoning proposal to the regular City Council (M05#1).

threads.name: Salem Street Corridor Rezoning
threads.summary: The committee initiated discussions on Salem Street corridor zoning updates in August 2024, reviewing recommendations for density nodes up to six stories at major intersections alongside residential-only blocks to preserve neighborhood character (M01#3, M01#4). Consultants delivered status updates and draft sub-districts under Paper 24-033 in late 2024 to correct high-rise loopholes and support commercial nodes (M06#2, M07#1, M07#2). In December 2024, the committee reviewed a refined proposal featuring multi-unit and mixed-use districts that grant height bonuses in exchange for deeper affordability and public parking, voting to refer the proposal to the City Council (M08#1). The public engagement timeline continued into early 2025 with public question-and-answer sessions and Community Development Board reviews (M10#1).

threads.name: Neighborhood and Urban Residential Zoning
threads.summary: In January 2025, consultants presented a citywide framework to replace single-family zoning with tiered neighborhood residential zones allowing accessory units and historic conversions, prompting the committee to vote to scale down proposed density tiers across several neighborhoods (M09#1, M09#2). Subsequent revisions established five residential sub-districts capped at three stories, incorporating protections to ensure existing single-family homes would not face unnecessary variance burdens for minor renovations (M11#1, M11#3). In February 2025, the committee reviewed the finalized draft text and voted to refer the residential zoning proposal to the regular City Council for subsequent referral to the Community Development Board (M12#2, M12#7). In July 2025, Council President Zac Bears proposed a revised project timeline extending the detailed review of residential districts and parking requirements into 2026 to prioritize commercial and institutional zoning updates (M20#1).

threads.name: Commercial Squares Rezoning
threads.summary: In March 2025, consultants introduced a citywide commercial framework creating three mixed-use sub-districts and detailed height profiles and sunlight protections for Medford Square (M13#1, M14#1). The committee held an initial review of West Medford Square in April 2025, evaluating proposals to replace existing commercial districts with mixed-use and urban residential zones near the commuter rail stop (M15#1). Later that month, the committee finalized revised maps establishing daylight standards for Medford Square and designating Mixed Use 2B as the primary district in West Medford Square, voting to refer both proposals favorably to the City Council (M16#1, M16#2, M16#4). In April 2026, the committee directed planning staff to advance a 40R Smart Growth strategy for Medford Square to leverage state reimbursement funding for the city's high school building project (M24#4, M24#5).

threads.name: Boston Avenue and Tufts Institutional District Rezoning
threads.summary: The committee began preliminary discussions on minor corridors and Tufts University campus zoning in mid-2025, voting to report an initial corridors draft out of committee while keeping institutional zoning frameworks in committee for further research (M17#2, M19#1, M19#3, M20#4). In April 2026, the committee resumed work on Boston Avenue and the university area, examining how Dover Amendment limitations affect municipal authority over campus buildings and reviewing parcel non-conformity data (M24#1, M24#3, M25#1). Members discussed district scope, taxable private student housing in the O2 zone, and alignment with Medford Square dimensional standards (M24#2, M25#3, M25#4). In May 2026, the committee reviewed a draft creating three mixed-use sub-districts on Boston Avenue, approved an amendment prohibiting drive-throughs and gas stations, debated incentive heights, and voted to refer the amended draft to the City Council for joint review with the Community Development Board (M26#1, M26#2, M26#3, M26#7).

threads.name: Accessory Dwelling Unit Regulations
threads.summary: The committee tracked local accessory dwelling unit (ADU) regulations in response to state statutory mandates throughout early 2025 (M11#3, M12#3). In March 2025, members reviewed draft updates and expressed support for permitting ADUs across all residential districts, prohibiting short-term rentals, and designating the Community Development Board as the special permit granting authority (M13#2). A refined draft addressed specific dimensional standards, including setback requirements, height limits, and special permit criteria for second units on a single parcel (M14#2). In April 2025, the committee concluded its review of the regulations, establishing special permit rules for second ADUs and units in historic accessory structures, and voted to refer the ADU proposal favorably to the City Council (M16#3, M16#4).

threads.name: Environmental Performance and Green Score
threads.summary: In September 2024, the committee formed a consensus to develop a 100-point green score rubric focused on heat mitigation and landscape functionality for projects subject to site plan review (M02#1). Paula Ramos Martinez presented performance standards and a landscape score menu in November 2024, which the committee voted to refer to the regular City Council meeting (M06#1). Green score incentives were subsequently embedded into development standards for major corridors to promote active frontages and environmental performance (M19#4). In May 2026, the committee incorporated an elevated 25-point green score requirement into the draft Boston Avenue corridor zoning to incentivize bioswales and larger shade trees (M26#4).

threads.name: Property Oversight and Housing Protection Ordinances
threads.summary: In September 2024, staff clarified that condominium conversion rules fall under general city ordinances rather than zoning by-laws (M02#3). Chair Kit Collins introduced a preliminary draft condominium conversion ordinance in December 2025 that proposed tenant relocation payments and a review board, which was kept in committee for further executive consultation (M21#1). In January 2026, the committee reviewed a draft vacant commercial properties ordinance featuring an escalating fee structure and online registry, voting to keep it in committee for legal review (M22#1). In March 2026, the committee reviewed revisions establishing tiered registration fees and property management definitions, voting to refer the vacant building ordinance to the City Council pending final legal review (M23#2).
